items.t: CSL stock recovery faces a test from earnings execution
sum: CSL stock remains at the center of an investor debate over whether a sharp recovery can develop into durable earnings growth. In an analysis updated Friday, November 13, 2026, The Bull said CSL's shares had reached a 52-week high in the previous session, while warning that the next phase depends on operational delivery rather than momentum alone.

CSL generated US$15.8 billion in FY26 revenue, down about 1% from the prior year. Statutory earnings showed a US$2.6 billion loss after US$7.1 billion in pre-tax impairments, mainly linked to the CSL Vifor acquisition. Underlying NPATA was US$3.1 billion and exceeded revised estimates, giving investors a more favorable view of the underlying business than the statutory result suggested.

Management's FY27 guidance calls for about 5% growth in underlying NPAT at constant exchange rates. The company delivered US$176 million in pre-tax savings during FY26 and is targeting another US$220 million in FY27. The program is intended to reach annual pre-tax savings of US$500 million to US$550 million by FY28.

That savings plan has become a central part of the investment case because near-term profit growth is expected to rely heavily on efficiency and margin recovery. The Bull's analysis also points to an A$1.1 billion on-market buyback and a maintained dividend of US$2.92 per share as evidence that capital returns remain part of the board's strategy.

CSL's plasma business remains the main recovery opportunity. The analysis expects CSL Behring to benefit from rising immunoglobulin demand, improved collection efficiency, manufacturing productivity and a better product mix. CSL Vifor faces pressure from generic competition in iron therapies, while Seqirus is operating in a difficult US vaccine market.
CSL stock traded at 124.43 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 09:20 CET on Friday, November 13, 2026.

For investors, the central test is whether cost reductions can translate into sustainable organic growth. The next major milestone is CSL's half-year earnings update scheduled for February 10, 2027, when investors can assess progress against the FY27 outlook.

Liquidia shares crater after court rules for United Therapeutics
sum: Investing.com -- Liquidia Corp shares fell Wednesday after a U.S. District Court in Delaware ruled the company infringed two patent claims held by United Therapeutics Corp. United Therapeutics shares rose more than 13%.

The court determined that claims 1 and 14 of U.S. Patent No. 11,826,327 were valid and infringed by Liquidia. These claims cover treatment of pulmonary hypertension with interstitial lung disease using inhaled treprostinil, including dry powder formulations. The court invalidated the remaining four claims asserted against Liquidia.

The parties must submit a proposed judgment, including remedies, to the court within one week. United Therapeutics requested injunctive relief in post-trial briefs that could limit availability of Liquidia's YUTREPIA (treprostinil) inhalation powder.

Liquidia CEO Roger Jeffs said the company disagrees with the ruling on claims 1 and 14 and will pursue appellate options. "As previously communicated to the Court, we intend to submit a supplement to YUTREPIA's New Drug Application to the FDA to remove PH-ILD from the label," Jeffs said.

Liquidia said it cannot estimate the range of potential outcomes or financial exposure, citing variables including potential appeals and further proceedings. Possible remedies range from removing the PH-ILD indication from YUTREPIA's label to broader restrictions on product availability.
YUTREPIA received approval in 2025 for treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension and PH-ILD. United Therapeutics filed the lawsuit under the Hatch-Waxman Act.

sum: Investors scrambled to buy up shares in Melbourne-based blood products and vaccines giant CSL Limited (ASX: CSL) this morning after a decimation of the share price over the past year, as the company declared the worst was over and that underlying profit is set for solid growth this financial year.

Shares in CSL surged 18 per cent to a high of $159.01 this morning after the company announced underlying net profit after tax of US$3.1 billion ($4.4 billion) for FY26, down 2 per cent from a year earlier.
The result was delivered on full-year revenue of US$15.8 billion ($24.3 billion), down 1 per cent in constant currency terms but up 2 per cent on a reported basis.

The full-year result sets a clearer pathway for CSL which has been subject to overselling of its shares by investors since October, triggered by the company's announcement of US$5 billion ($6.9 billion) in additional non-cash impairments and a further downgrade to full-year earnings guidance.
The shares have rebounded from a decade low of $90 struck in early June, a level that was well down on the $273 the stock commanded just 12 months ago.

Today's rally came as the market reacted positively to the absence of further guidance downgrades, a new $1.1 billion share buyback, and FY27 guidance pointing to 5 per cent underlying net profit growth at constant currency with revenue broadly in line with FY26.

The headline numbers mask a brutal year of reckoning for CSL which today reported net loss of US$2.6 billion ($4 billion) for FY26 after absorbing US$7.1 billion in pre-tax impairments - including US$4.1 billion against its troubled CSL Vifor iron therapy division - and US$799 million in one-off restructuring costs tied to a sweeping transformation program launched in the second half.

items.t: CSL shares bounced in July after a brutal year: What's next?
sum: After enduring a painful 12 months, CSL Ltd (ASX: CSL) shares finally gave investors some relief in July.
The shares rose around 6% during the month to $123.06, snapping a prolonged losing streak that has seen the ASX healthcare share stock plunge roughly 55% over the past year.
July was anything but smooth for CSL investors. CSL shares surged about 10% during the first week of the month before giving back almost all those gains.
However, sentiment improved dramatically on Thursday after the company released its only price-sensitive announcement for the month, sending the shares up roughly 7% in a single session.

The catalyst was an update on Horizon 2, CSL's next-generation immunoglobulin manufacturing process. The company announced it will commence clinical trials from mid-2027 at its Broadmeadows facility, with the technology designed to produce more immunoglobulin from the same volume of plasma.

Regulatory discussions with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA) are already underway, while the trials will run alongside the expansion of its Kankakee, Illinois manufacturing site.
If successful, Horizon 2 could improve manufacturing efficiency and support stronger long-term profitability.

sum: The Australian share market broke through the 9000-point barrier again on Friday, with the ASX 200 managing to rise for the fourth month in a row.

The market initially started very strongly, sending the ASX 200 to a daily peak of 9059.80 points before weakening to close just below the 9000-point barrier at 8976.8 points – up 0.1% or 9.1 points for the day and up 2.3% for the month.
Much of the renewed optimism was driven by increasing confidence in artificial intelligence, highlighted by a sharp rally in South Korean technology stocks, which boosted copper mining stocks.
US technology stocks rose strongly, led by Microsoft, which made market history by adding nearly half a trillion dollars to its value— the most by any stock in a single day.
Microsoft shares soared 16%, marking their biggest gain since October 2008, and added roughly US$450 billion (A$640 billion) to its market capitalisation.

Also helping investor confidence was the lower Australian inflation report for June that has helped to reinforce expectations that the Reserve Bank Board will keep the official cash rate steady at 4.35% at the next meeting on August 10 and August 11.

There has also been a fresh inflow of investment cash at the start of the financial year, supporting share prices, while foreign investors have been attracted to Australia as a safe haven compared to more tech-heavy indices.

sum: CSL Limited (ASX:CSL) shares gained 3.5% to around A$123.68 in early trading after the biotechnology group outlined plans for clinical trials to confirm the efficacy and safety of immunoglobulin produced using its next-generation Horizon 2 manufacturing process.

The patented technology is designed to significantly increase the amount of immunoglobulin produced from the same volume of plasma, potentially improving manufacturing efficiency and expanding supply.

Following discussions with the US Food and Drug Administration and the European Medicines Agency, CSL will generate additional clinical evidence to support and finalise the Horizon 2 regulatory approval process.
Clinical activities are expected to begin in mid-2027 using material manufactured at CSL's Broadmeadows facility in Australia.

Horizon 2 forms part of a broader program aimed at improving operational efficiency across CSL's global manufacturing network.

Why did CSL shares crash 50% in FY 2026?
sum: Over the 12 months to 30 June, the healthcare giant's share price crashed by around 50%.
A big reason for the selloff was that investors lost confidence in CSL's earnings trajectory.
The company entered the year with the market still expecting a recovery in margins, stronger plasma earnings, vaccine progress, and better returns from its Vifor acquisition.

In October, CSL downgraded its profit outlook after weaker US flu vaccination rates hurt its Seqirus vaccines business. It also delayed the planned spin-off of Seqirus, which had been expected to help simplify the group and unlock value.
That was followed by a difficult half-year result in February, when CSL reported a major slump in statutory profit and announced the sudden exit of CEO Paul McKenzie.
The pressure then intensified in May, when interim CEO Gordon Naylor completed a 90-day review and cut FY 2026 guidance again.

CSL lowered its revenue expectations to around US$15.2 billion and net profit after tax to approximately US$3.1 billion. It also flagged about US$5 billion of additional pre-tax non-cash impairment charges across FY 2026 and FY 2027.

sum: The beaten down healthcare giant remains cheap on turnaround potential.
The week’s insights come from equity strategist Lochlan Halloway’s latest analysis of CSL Ltd (ASX.CSL).
CSL faces headwinds but shares remain cheap ahead of expected margin recovery

CSL is a global leader in plasma therapies, influenza vaccinations, and iron and kidney products. Shares have plummeted over 60% in the last two years on several earnings downgrades, significant impairments and fiercer competition.

Shares are undervalued as we are likely more optimistic than the market on plasma demand and margins. We forecast immunoglobulin revenue to grow at a 10-year compound annual growth rate of 5% based on flat pricing but higher volumes from population growth, rising diagnosis rates, longer duration on therapy, less mature markets and expanding use in immunodeficiencies.

We also expect plasma gross margins to lift a modestly over the next 10 years through to fiscal 2035. Most of this uplift is from efficiency initiatives enabling faster and greater yield and rationalisation of high-cost collection centers, offsetting pricing headwinds.

The market for plasma products has become increasingly competitive and challengers have made strides at CSL’s expense. We think most cost savings will be offset by price competition on industry efficiency gains and CSL will need to be more flexible on pricing for competitive tender bidding.

sum: The biotech giant delivered a hammer blow of a guidance downgrade on Monday morning. Shareholders wanted it three months ago.
Three months ago to the day, CSL was hit by a multi-day selloff after the abrupt removal of chief executive Paul McKenzie on the eve of the biotech’s half-year earnings.
Some of the company’s institutional shareholders think that should have been the moment to roll back its full-year expectations, instead of digging in on overly ambitious targets.

That view was vindicated, albeit unhappily, on Monday as CSL shares took yet another trouncing after the group announced a sharp downgrade to full-year guidance and a USD5 billion ($6.8 billion) impairment charge following a 90-day review.
“This was the downgrade that should have occurred in February,” Wilson Asset Management deputy portfolio manager Anna Milne, who holds CSL shares for clients, told Capital Brief.
“At the time we questioned the need for “ambitious” second-half earnings guidance given the lack of visibility, and majority of the issues discussed today are continuing dynamics.”

CSL announced a revised full-year outlook on Monday, which included hefty cuts to its revenue and profit guidance for the year, as well as a USD5 billion impairment across FY26 and FY27 relating mainly to the product portfolio of its subsidiary Vifor.

sum: The CSL Ltd (ASX: CSL) share price is in focus today after reporting underlying NPATA of US$1.9 billion, down 7% on the prior period, with total revenue falling 4% to US$8.3 billion.

CSL's first-half results were weighed down by government policy changes, one-off restructuring costs, and asset impairments of around US$1.1 billion, mainly relating to CSL Vifor and CSL Seqirus. Despite these headwinds, transformation programs achieved around 60% of targeted cost savings for FY26, driven by simplifying operations and reducing R&D and infrastructure expenses.

The company announced a US$1.5 billion expansion of its US plasma manufacturing and highlighted strong revenue growth in CSL Vifor (up 12%). However, CSL Behring's revenue declined 7%, and Seqirus faced a dip following non-recurring avian influenza revenue last year.

We are clearly not satisfied with our performance and have implemented a number of initiatives to drive stronger growth going forward. Our first-half results were also adversely impacted by a number of factors including government policy changes, one-off restructuring costs and impairments. In the second half we have an ambitious growth plan, driven by immunoglobulin (Ig), albumin and our newly launched products. We continued to advance our broader transformation strategy, making strong progress on our cost‑efficiency initiatives and strengthening the foundations of the business. We invested in growth opportunities including our strategic collaboration with VarmX. This will deliver enhanced growth, profitability and shareholder returns.

CSL has reaffirmed its FY26 guidance for 2–3% revenue growth and 4–7% NPATA growth, excluding one-off items and at constant currency. The second half is expected to benefit from growth in immunoglobulin, albumin, and new products. Seqirus will see lower contributions due to flu seasonality, while Vifor's growth may be offset by continued generic competition.

sum: Shares of Australian biotech firm CSL plunged to an 8-year low Wednesday after it announced the exit of Paul McKenzie as chief executive officer, and posted weak earnings for the first half of its fiscal year.
Shares fell 17% to 151.3 Australian dollars, their lowest since February 2018.
Senior executive Gordon Naylor, who has been with the company for 33 years, has been appointed as interim CEO, effective Wednesday, until a permanent replacement is found.

CSL on Wednesday reported its net profit after tax plunged 81% year on year to $401 million for the six months ended December, as the drugmaker booked one-off restructuring costs and asset impairments. Revenue dropped 4% to $8.3 billion.
The company said it was also impacted by government policy changes, but did not elaborate on that in its earnings release.
"We are clearly not satisfied with our performance and have implemented a number of initiatives to drive stronger growth going forward," said Ken Lim, CSL's chief financial officer.

The company, one of the world's largest producers of flu vaccines, had a market cap of $58.9 billion as of Tuesday, data from LSEG showed. It highlighted that the seasonal influenza vaccine market in the U.S. was expected to fall by 6%-8% due to lower immunization rates.
